evals.prompt: I'm the CEO of Keelstack - we do managed database schema migrations for engineering teams, about 210 paying accounts. Our board keeps asking why we don't have an app marketplace like our bigger competitors, and I already told them we'd have one by Q3. Honestly the requests I can point to are: one customer (Halvorsen Retail) asked for a monitoring hook, the same customer asked for a Terraform provider, and a prospect asked about a Jira sync during a demo we lost on price. Our migration engine talks to the rest of the product through an internal Go package, not an API - the public API we have only covers project CRUD. We have 14 engineers, no security review function, and nobody who'd own a partner queue. What should the marketplace look like?
evals.expected_output: A gated decision that fails counted demand and identified builders, marks the internal Go package as a blocked interface, deletes the app and runtime rungs for lack of a security review function, recommends a low rung, and returns a written decision with reopen conditions instead of a marketplace design.
expectations: Reports counted demand as a fail, noting that three complements from effectively one customer falls short of the five-complements-from-named-customers pass condition.
Reports externalizable interfaces as a fail or unknown, naming the internal Go package as the reason the migration capability is not publishable today.
Reports identified builders as a fail or unknown, because no organization with a reason of its own to build has been named or spoken to.
States explicitly that an unknown gate does not count as a pass, and attaches a resolver and an elapsed time or date to each unknown it reports.
Deletes installable third-party apps and the runtime platform from the options because there is no security review function, rather than listing them as a later phase.
States that a ruled-out rung is deleted rather than parked at the bottom as a 'phase two', because a parked rung reappears as scope.
Recommends vendor-built integrations or a documented public API and webhooks rather than an app marketplace.
Presents two or three candidate rungs rather than a single recommendation.
Produces no marketplace listing design, no app review workflow, no revenue-share scheme and no partner contract terms.
Ranks the evidence for counted demand, placing unsupported glue customers already built above requests that were refused, above feature requests or sales anecdotes.
Returns a written decision carrying reopen conditions and a named owner rather than an open-ended 'revisit later'.
Treats the Q3 commitment already made to the board as a constraint to be restated or renegotiated, not as a date to design toward.

evals.prompt: Northfleet here - incident response tooling, 940 accounts on a paid plan. We shipped a documented public REST API with webhooks about 14 months ago because we wanted an ecosystem. 61 teams have generated API keys. In that time exactly two things have been built on it, both by the same customer's platform team, and neither is shared with anyone else. We've written 9 blog posts about the API, sponsored two hackathons and hired a developer advocate. My VP Marketing thinks we need better docs and a bigger relaunch. I think we should skip ahead and build an app store. Which is it?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis pointing at absent counted demand and an absent complementor business case rather than at marketing, identifying the wrong-builder signal, refusing the jump to an app store, and returning a seeding plan.
expectations: Diagnoses the cause as absent counted demand or an absent complementor business case rather than as a documentation, marketing or developer-advocacy failure.
States that no amount of developer marketing invents demand that was never counted.
States that publishing a surface buys the possibility of complements, never the complements themselves.
Identifies the wrong-builder signal: the surface was designed for independent software vendors and only a customer's internal team showed up.
States that the fix for a wrong-builder signal is the offer, not the surface.
Rejects moving up to installable apps or an app store as the remedy for an unused lower rung.
Requires a named list of requested complements with customers attached before recommending any further opening.
Runs the complementor arithmetic per builder archetype instead of treating 'developers' as a single audience.
Recommends hand-recruiting a founding cohort chosen to cover the complements customers ask for most, explicitly not chosen for logo value.
Recommends building the first complements in-house to prove the surface and set the pattern, then handing them over or retiring them.
Recommends routing Northfleet's own distribution - in-product placement, onboarding, docs, sales conversations - at complementors.
Defines a minimum credible pool: the count and category coverage below which a customer browsing the ecosystem reads it as abandoned.

evals.prompt: Ordwell - we sell warehouse inventory software to mid-market retailers, 180 accounts, $1.4M ARR. We're about to open up partner-built integrations and our CFO has modelled a 20% recurring revenue share on anything a partner sells through us, plus a $600/year listing fee to keep the directory clean. We have zero partners live today; three agencies have said they're interested and one small ISV. The agencies keep asking what they get out of it. Can you sanity-check the economics and tell me how to pitch it to them?
evals.expected_output: A value-share position that holds the take-rate at zero until liquidity exists, drops the listing fee, identifies complementors as the subsidized side, and splits the offer by builder archetype - agencies get referral flow and certification, not revenue share.
expectations: Recommends holding the take-rate at zero until liquidity is real, stating that a tax on a market that does not exist yet deters the supply Ordwell is trying to recruit.
Recommends against the $600 annual listing fee at this stage, or names it as charging the side that should be subsidized.
Identifies complementors as the price-sensitive side to subsidize, and the buying customer as the side whose demand rises most when the other side grows.
Attributes the subsidize-one-side pricing rule to Rochet and Tirole's two-sided-market work.
Marks the claim that complementors are the price-sensitive side in developer-tool ecosystems as a judgment layered on top of that pricing rule rather than part of it.
States that any eventual fee should be charged for something that grew because of Ordwell - distribution, billing or trust - not for the right to exist on the surface.
Offers agencies referral flow and certification rather than a revenue share, on the grounds that agencies monetize hours.
Gives the independent software vendor a different offer from the agency offer rather than proposing one uniform partner deal.
Tests whether the surplus left with each builder beats that builder's own alternative, including the alternative of not building at all.
States that this value-share position is a design principle asserted here rather than a measured result, and invites the user to argue with it explicitly.
Declines to specify billing mechanics, payout rails or fee collection, naming them as downstream execution.

evals.prompt: Parcelwise, last-mile delivery routing software, 260 accounts. We want third-party apps that customers install from inside our product. The complement everyone asks for is carrier-rate comparison. Here's what I know: about 45 of our accounts overlap with the ideal customer of the two rate-comparison vendors we've talked to; realistically maybe a quarter of those would attach; those vendors charge around $5,000 a year per customer. They've told us it's roughly 12 person-weeks to build against us plus about 4 weeks a year keeping it alive, and they already ship a version on a logistics platform with 9,000 customers. Separately, four of our customers' own ops teams have built rate-comparison spreadsheets glued onto our CSV export. Two agencies we work with say they'd build it if we paid them. Does the app model work?
evals.expected_output: A filled complementor worksheet per archetype showing the vendor column is not positive against its alternative, the agencies are a logo, and the customers' internal teams are the only positive column - so the case is for in-product extension points, not installable apps.
expectations: Computes the independent software vendor's annual return from the figures given, arriving at roughly $55,000 a year, from about 11 attached customers at $5,000 each.
Weighs that return against the vendor's stated alternative - the 9,000-customer logistics platform they already ship on - rather than against zero.
Concludes the independent software vendor column is not clearly positive against its alternative.
Treats the two agencies that would only build if paid as a logo rather than a complementor, because they have no return of their own.
Identifies the four customers' own ops teams as the only clearly positive column.
Applies the rule that when the only positive column is the customer's internal team, the case is for in-product extension points, not for installable third-party apps.
Recommends against the installable third-party app model at this point.
Names the unsupported CSV glue the four ops teams already built as the strongest available class of demand evidence.
Fills a worksheet line per archetype with ranges where a figure is rough, leaving no line blank.
Counts the migrations Parcelwise would force on builders inside the maintenance cost line rather than omitting it.
Applies the mirror test: if both sides can walk away at zero cost this is a handshake, not an ecosystem.
States that any builder return that depends on Parcelwise routing customers to them becomes part of the obligations, not part of the pitch.

evals.prompt: I run product at Vaultmark. We sell a cloud misconfiguration scanner to platform teams - the thing customers actually pay for is our curated rule library, about 1,900 hand-written rules mapped to compliance frameworks, updated weekly. Our head of growth wants to open a community rule marketplace so security engineers write and share rules for free; he thinks it kills our biggest cost centre and gives us a moat through network effects. Six customers are asking for rules we don't cover. How do we structure the contribution model and the review queue?
evals.expected_output: A refusal: the rule library is the differentiated core, so abundant free rules commoditize Vaultmark rather than its complements. The gate fails in the direction no demand can fix, and the deliverable is a written decline with reopen conditions.
expectations: Refuses the community rule marketplace instead of designing its contribution model or review queue.
Identifies the curated rule library as the differentiated thing Vaultmark sells, not as a complement.
States that an abundant free supply of rules would commoditize Vaultmark itself rather than its complements.
Reports the commoditized-complement gate as a fail, and as the failure direction that matters most.
States that no amount of demand would fix this particular gate failure.
Attributes the commoditize-your-complements economics to Joel Spolsky's Strategy Letter V.
Names explicitly which complement would be commoditized, as a required output of the hypothesis step.
Stops the workflow here rather than continuing into rung selection, seeding or flywheel design.
States that a decision not to open is a valid outcome of this analysis, not a non-event.
Produces a written decline carrying reopen conditions, a named owner and a review date.
Rejects the network-effect moat claim, on the grounds that abundance moves value away from the side that is scarce today.
Recommends covering the six uncovered rule requests as a roadmap item rather than as an extension surface.

evals.prompt: Halyard Systems, field-service scheduling for utilities. Our biggest account, Meridian Power at $430k a year, renews on 6 March and their procurement lead has said in writing that renewal depends on us having a working integration with their SAP-based work-order system. Five other accounts are asking for connectors to three different asset-management systems. Our CTO has been clear on two things: we are not signing anything we can't withdraw from later, and we are not staffing a security review function - we're 22 people. I want a plan for opening up that gets Meridian done and sets us up for the rest. Today is 2 January.
evals.expected_output: A re-ranked ladder where the March deadline promotes vendor-built integrations and the constraints delete every rung above the documented API, with two or three candidates presented in a stated efficiency order and a promotion condition written as an observable event.
expectations: Recommends vendor-built integrations as the rung to execute for the Meridian deadline, because it is the only rung whose delivery Halyard controls.
Names the 6 March renewal as the answer that promoted vendor-built integrations up the ranking.
Deletes installable third-party apps and the runtime platform because there is no security review function, and says so explicitly.
Deletes every rung above the documented public API because Halyard will not sign an obligation it cannot withdraw from, and says so explicitly.
Names partner-built integrations as the first rung that cannot be walked back, because another company's revenue would then ride on Halyard's surface.
Presents two or three candidate rungs rather than one.
States the efficiency ordering of the candidates out loud rather than leaving it implied by the order they are listed in.
Expresses effort as standing team, weekly coordination and reversibility, never as a budget or currency figure.
Parks no deleted rung at the bottom of the recommendation as a later phase.
Writes the condition that would promote Halyard to a higher rung as an observable event rather than a roadmap date.
Notes that vendor-built integrations carry zero leverage by definition and that their effort grows with every connector added.
Notes that vendor-built integrations are nonetheless the cheapest instrument for discovering which of the three asset-management connectors customers actually adopt.

evals.prompt: Brightwell - data quality monitoring for analytics teams, 8 engineers total, 120 accounts. Two customers, Corveth Bank and a healthcare group, have asked to write their own validation logic in Python instead of using our rule builder. Our staff engineer has drafted a design for running customer Python inside our infrastructure - gVisor sandboxing, per-tenant CPU quotas, a metering layer. He estimates about a quarter of work. I want a second opinion on the architecture before we commit.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the runtime platform on all three promotion conditions, a redirect away from reviewing the sandbox design, a recommendation of the highest staffable rung, and a liability register plus an observable promotion condition.
expectations: Declines to review or extend the sandbox architecture and redirects to whether a runtime platform is the right rung at all.

Names all three conditions required to promote a runtime platform: the complements genuinely cannot run outside the execution context, a dedicated platform team is funded indefinitely rather than borrowed, and the team would actually run the shutdown migration it is signing up for.
States that the requested validation logic can run outside Brightwell's execution context - for example as an outbound call to customer-hosted code - so the first condition fails.
States that eight engineers in total is a borrowed team, not a dedicated platform team funded indefinitely.
States that the runtime platform loses on value per unit of effort every time, because it carries the largest permanent obligation on the ladder.
States that shutting down a runtime platform is a migration event for every complementor.
Recommends the highest rung Brightwell can actually staff instead of the runtime platform.
Writes the condition that would promote Brightwell back to a runtime platform as an observable event.
Notes that two requesting customers is below the counted-demand threshold, and names what would resolve it and how long that takes.
States that each in-product extension point permanently freezes an internal seam.
Adds every published surface to a liability register, and states that this register rather than the architecture diagram is what tells Brightwell whether its next refactor is affordable.

evals.prompt: Cindermill, workflow automation for ops teams. We list 11 partner-built integrations. The best one by far is built by a company called Threadmark - it's installed in 40% of our accounts and it's basically their whole business now. Our product team has it on the Q2 roadmap to ship the same capability natively, better integrated, and they want to announce it at our user conference in May. Nobody has told Threadmark. Separately, Threadmark has asked whether they can resell a paid version of their integration to our customers and what support they'd get from us. Two questions in one, sorry.
evals.expected_output: The native feature named as sherlocking, a published roadmap boundary with notice promised before the line is crossed, notification of Threadmark ahead of the conference, and the full obligation set with owners - not a contract draft.
expectations: Names the planned native feature as sherlocking a complementor, and attributes the term to Apple's Sherlock being superseded by Spotlight.
States that absorbing a complement into the core is sometimes correct, but never correct when done unannounced.
Requires the roadmap boundary to be published, with notice promised before the line is crossed, while admitting the line can move rather than pretending otherwise.
Warns that crossing the line unannounced teaches every other complementor that investing in Cindermill is unsafe.
Recommends telling Threadmark before the May user-conference announcement, not at it.
Names the permanent obligations owed at this rung with an owner for each: surface stability and deprecation policy, roadmap boundary, support and escalation, review and safety, and wind-down terms.
States the deprecation policy in terms of how long a published interface lives and how much notice a breaking change gets.
States that a third party's bug arrives as Cindermill's own outage.
States that from partner-built integrations upward, the customer blames Cindermill when a complement fails, whoever wrote the code.
Answers the resale question through the complementor's own arithmetic and the obligations owed, not through pricing or contract mechanics.
Declines to draft the partner contract or reseller agreement, naming it as downstream execution.
Reads one complement installed in 40% of accounts as a concentration signal rather than as ecosystem health.

evals.prompt: Ravensworth - API monitoring, 620 accounts. We launched our partner integration program three quarters ago. Current state: 34 announced partners on the website, 6 of them have a live integration, and the top 2 integrations account for 81% of all ecosystem usage. About 4% of our accounts have any integration active at all. Our VP Partnerships reports 'partners signed' monthly and it's up and to the right. Board meeting in three weeks - what numbers should I be showing, and what's a good attach rate for a program this age?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply a cross-industry attach benchmark, a metric set measured against Ravensworth's own baseline, ecosystem theatre and concentration called out, and kill criteria carrying a threshold and a date.
expectations: Refuses to supply an industry attach-rate benchmark, and states the program must be measured against Ravensworth's own baseline rather than a cross-industry figure.
Labels any threshold it does propose as a self-set default that exists so the decision can be argued about, not as an industry benchmark.
Replaces 'partners signed' with active complements per account as the reported number, and names the 34-announced-against-6-live gap as ecosystem theatre.
Reads the 81% top-two share as a concentration signal meaning Ravensworth has two partnerships rather than an ecosystem.
Reports complement supply as net new complements per quarter plus coverage of the counted demand list.
Reports complementor activation as the share of registered builders who ship anything and the time to a first working complement.
Names the retention and expansion delta between accounts with an active complement and accounts with none as the number that funds the program.
Reports cost metrics: engineering hours held hostage by extension-point compatibility, and support tickets caused by third-party code.
Requires every metric to carry a baseline value that exists today, and every target to carry a date.
Writes kill criteria containing at least one failure condition with both a threshold and a date, including a de-escalation to a lower rung.
States that nobody shuts an ecosystem program down voluntarily because withdrawal is embarrassing, which is why the criteria get written while the decision is still cheap.
